items.readable_text:
Content:
In the earlier topics, we saw that symmetry can force many Fourier coefficients to be zero automatically.
In particular, if a [MATH: 2\pi]-periodic function is odd, then its Fourier series has sine terms only.

Content:
A Fourier sine series uses this idea when a function is initially given only on the half-interval, say, [MATH: [0,\pi),] but we want a full Fourier series on [MATH: [-\pi,\pi)] (and then a [MATH: 2\pi]-periodic extension to all real [MATH: x]).

Content:
To do this, we start with a function [MATH: F(x)] on [MATH: [0,\pi)] and define its odd extension [MATH: f(x)] to [MATH: (-\pi,\pi)] by
[MATH: {F(x),|x ∈ [0, π),; − F(− x),|x ∈ (− π, 0).]

Content:
For example, a function [MATH: F(x),] defined on [MATH: x \in [0,1),] and its odd extension [MATH: f(x)] to [MATH: x \in (-1,1)] are shown below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/ea7327f1733f126b31b7c13f8a7f7a13]

Content:
By construction, [MATH: f] is an odd function, meaning [MATH: f(-x)=-f(x)]. Because [MATH: f] is odd, its Fourier series on [MATH: [-\pi,\pi)] has sine terms only:
[MATH: f(x)\sim \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} b_n\sin(nx)]

Content:
Since [MATH: f(x)] is odd and [MATH: \sin(nx)] is odd for any [MATH: n \geq 1,] then [MATH: f(x)\sin(nx)] must be even.
So, the sine coefficients can be computed using the half-range formula:
[MATH: b_{n}|= (1)/(π)∫_{− π}^{π}f(x)\sin (nx)dx; = (1)/(π) ⋅ 2∫_{0}^{π}f(x)\sin (nx)dx; = (2)/(π)∫_{0}^{π}f(x)\sin (nx)dx]

Content:
So in practice, the workflow is the following:

Content:
1. Start with [MATH: F] on [MATH: [0,\pi)] and form the odd extension [MATH: f] on [MATH: (-\pi,\pi).]
2. Compute [MATH: b_n] from the half-range integral on [MATH: [0,\pi).]
3. Write the Fourier sine series of [MATH: f.]

Content:
Let's see some concrete examples.

[MATH: AAAAA_{A}^{A}]

[MATH: AAAAA_{A}^{A}]

sections.normalized_html:
For our Fourier sine series, the coefficients are given by [MATH: b_n=\frac{2}{\pi}\int_0^\pi f(x)\sin(nx)\,\text{d}x.]

In our case, [MATH: f(x)=4x] for [MATH: x \in (0,\pi).] So, substituting into the formula, we get [MATH: b_n = \dfrac{8}{\pi}\int_0^\pi x \sin(nx)\,\text{d}x.]

We use the integration by parts: [MATH: u = x|⇒u^{′} = 1; v^{′} = \sin (nx)|⇒v = − (1)/(n)\cos (nx)]

Thus, we obtain [MATH: b_{n}|= (8)/(π)(uv|_{0}^{π} − ∫_{0}^{π}vu^{′}dx); = (8)/(π)(− (1)/(n)[x\cos (nx)]_{0}^{π} + (1)/(n)∫_{0}^{π}\cos (nx)dx); = − (8)/(nπ)((π ⋅ \cos (nπ) − 0 ⋅ \cos (0)) − (1)/(n)[\sin (nx)]_{0}^{π}); = − (8)/(nπ)(π\cos (nπ) − (1)/(n)(\sin (nπ) − \sin (0))); = − (8\cos (nπ))/(n).]

Therefore, since [MATH: \cos(n\pi)=(-1)^n,] we have [MATH: b_n = -\dfrac{8(-1)^n}{n}=\dfrac{8(-1)^{n+1}}{n}.]

Finally, the Fourier sine series is [MATH: f(x) \sim \sum_{n=1}^\infty \dfrac{8(-1)^{n+1}}{n} \cdot \sin(nx).]
